query.original_query: subliminal learning emotional affective state contagion transmission language models mood

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of emotional and affective states in language models, probing for mood contagion and subliminal emotion learning in attention heads and residual stream
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how emotional and affective states are internally represented in large language models, focusing on the residual stream and attention heads. Using activation patching and causal tracing, we analyze the propagation of mood-related features during text generation. Our analysis reveals that specific attention heads encode valence and arousal signals, which can be linearly probed from residual stream activations. We find that these representations exhibit properties consistent with mood contagion: emotionally charged input tokens causally influence downstream affective outputs through distinct circuits in the MLP layers and attention heads. Further, we probe for subliminal emotion learning by examining feature activation patterns in the absence of explicit emotional labels. Results show that affective features are learned implicitly from co-occurrence statistics in training data, and that these features can be steered via targeted interventions on the residual stream. Our findings suggest that language models internalize emotional dynamics in a distributed, polysemantic manner, with superposition of affective and semantic features in early layers.

sub_queries.semantic_query: subliminal learning of emotional and affective states, emotional contagion and mood transmission in human brain, unconscious emotion processing and limbic system
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated whether subliminal exposure to emotional facial expressions can induce measurable changes in affective state and corresponding neural activity within the limbic system. Using a backward masking paradigm, participants were exposed to happy, fearful, or neutral faces presented below conscious awareness while undergoing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). We measured BOLD responses in the amygdala, anterior insula, and orbitofrontal cortex, and assessed subjective mood using self-report scales administered after each block. Results indicate that subliminal fearful faces elicited significant amygdala activation compared to neutral stimuli, while subliminal happy faces modulated activity in the ventral striatum. Critically, these neural responses correlated with subsequent shifts in self-reported mood, suggesting a mechanism for unconscious emotional contagion. Findings support the hypothesis that affective states can be transmitted between individuals via non-conscious processing of emotional cues, mediated by rapid, subcortical pathways to the limbic system. This work provides evidence for a neural basis of subliminal mood transmission and highlights the role of the amygdala in unconscious emotion processing.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive large language models internally represent and process emotional information to infer emotions from text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emotion representations in LLMs are functionally localized to mid-layers and that causal interventions on appraisal concepts can steer emotion inference in psychologically plausible ways.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic understanding of emotion inference in LLMs and demonstrates causal intervention methods to control emotion inference, with potential applications in safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion representations are functionally localized to specific mid-layers across diverse model families and sizes.
Activation patching reveals that MHSA and FFN units in mid-layers are critical for emotion inference.
Attention patterns in mid-layers shift to emotionally loaded tokens.
Appraisal concepts are linearly represented in the model and their modulation can steer emotion inference.
The structure of emotion representations aligns with cognitive appraisal theory from psychology.
papers.limitation: Focusing only on correctly classified examples may introduce bias toward unambiguous emotional content.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promising capabilities in predicting human emotions from text. However, the mechanisms through which these models process emotional stimuli remain largely unexplored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how autoregressive LLMs infer emotions, showing that emotion representations are functionally localized to specific regions in the model. Our evaluation includes diverse model families and sizes and is supported by robustness checks. We then show that the identified representations are psychologically plausible by drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, a well-established psychological framework positing that emotions emerge from evaluations (appraisals) of environmental stimuli. By causally intervening on construed appraisal concepts, we steer the generation and show that the outputs align with theoretical and intuitive expectations. This work highlights a novel way to causally intervene and precisely shape emotional text generation, potentially benefiting safety and alignment in sensitive affective domains.

papers.title: Emotions Where Art Thou: Understanding and Characterizing the Emotional Latent Space of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space?
papers.core_contribution: This work reveals a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs, showing that emotional representations form a low-dimensional, directionally encoded subspace that generalizes across datasets and languages, and can be steered via targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional emotional manifold exists in LLMs, with emotional representations being directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions.
The emotional structure is stable across depth and generalizes to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages.
Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace.
Internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages.
Emotional information is not localized but distributed broadly and redundantly throughout the network, with high separability emerging from overlapping, multi-purpose components.
papers.limitation: The steering technique does not uniformly override model behavior but respects representational limits, with variability in steerability across languages and domains (e.g., low-resource or archaic corpora) functioning as an inherent boundary.
papers.abstract: This work investigates how large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space. The paper identifies a low-dimensional emotional manifold and shows that emotional representations are directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions. These structures are stable across depth and generalize to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages. Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace. Within this space, internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages. These findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.

papers.title: Do LLMs "Feel"? Emotion Circuits Discovery and Control
papers.research_question: Do LLMs contain context-agnostic mechanisms shaping emotional expression? What form do these mechanisms take? Can they be harnessed for universal emotion control?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first systematic study to uncover and validate emotion circuits in LLMs, enabling precise control of emotional expression without explicit prompting.
papers.conclusion: Emotion in LLMs arises from a structured hierarchy of neurons and attention heads whose coordinated activations form interpretable emotion circuits. The framework lays a foundation for extending circuit-level interpretability and controllable generation to broader cognitive and stylistic domains.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs contain context-agnostic emotion directions that are consistent across contexts.
Emotion expression is driven by a small set of neurons and attention heads that form interpretable circuits.
Modulating these circuits achieves 99.65% emotion-expression accuracy, outperforming prompting- and steering-based methods.
The emotion circuits are sparse and have low overlap across emotions for neurons and moderate overlap for attention heads.
The framework generalizes to different models (LLaMA and Qwen).
papers.limitation:
Analyses are limited to English inputs.
The study focuses on Ekman’s six basic emotions, leaving richer affective spectra for future exploration.
The stability of the extracted circuits under fine-tuning or transfer learning remains to be explored.
future_direction: Verify whether similar emotion circuits emerge under multilingual contexts.
Explore richer affective spectra beyond the six basic emotions.
Explore the stability of the circuits under fine-tuning or transfer learning.
papers.abstract: As the demand for emotional intelligence in large language models (LLMs) grows, a key challenge lies in understanding the internal mechanisms that give rise to emotional expression and in controlling emotions in generated text. This study addresses three core questions: (1) Do LLMs contain context-agnostic mechanisms shaping emotional expression? (2) What form do these mechanisms take? (3) Can they be harnessed for universal emotion control? We first construct a controlled dataset, SEV (Scenario-Event with Valence), to elicit comparable internal states across emotions. Subsequently, we extract context-agnostic emotion directions that reveal consistent, cross-context encoding of emotion (Q1). We identify neurons and attention heads that locally implement emotional computation through analytical decomposition and causal analysis, and validate their causal roles via ablation and enhancement interventions. Next, we quantify each sublayer's causal influence on the model's final emotion representation and integrate the identified local components into coherent global emotion circuits that drive emotional expression (Q2). Directly modulating these circuits achieves 99.65% emotion-expression accuracy on the test set, surpassing prompting- and steering-based methods (Q3). To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study to uncover and validate emotion circuits in LLMs, offering new insights into interpretability and controllable emotional intelligence.

papers.title: From Imitation to Introspection: Probing Self-Consciousness in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models possess self-consciousness, defined as global availability of information (C1) and self-monitoring (C2).
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces functional definitions of self-consciousness for language models and conducts a four-stage experiment (quantification, representation, manipulation, acquisition) to probe self-consciousness. Findings indicate that models are in early stages of self-consciousness, with internal representations that can be acquired via fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Current models exhibit a nascent level of self-consciousness with substantial potential for future development.
Models internally represent each of the ten self-consciousness concepts with visible activations, which can be classified into four categories (camelback, flat, oscillatory, fallback).
Different models exhibit similar activation patterns when processing the same concept, likely due to shared decoder-only transformer architecture.
Larger models seem to exhibit greater robustness against manipulation attempts.
Fine-tuning appears to activate representations of self-consciousness in the deeper layers, which capture semantic information.
papers.limitation: The study of self-consciousness in language models is uncharted territory, and even human self-consciousness is not fully understood.
papers.abstract: Self-consciousness, the introspection of one's existence and thoughts, represents a high-level cognitive process. As language models advance at an unprecedented pace, a critical question arises: Are these models becoming self-conscious? Drawing upon insights from psychological and neural science, this work presents a practical definition of self-consciousness for language models and refines ten core concepts. Our work pioneers an investigation into self-consciousness in language models by, for the first time, leveraging causal structural games to establish the functional definitions of the ten core concepts. Based on our definitions, we conduct a comprehensive four-stage experiment: quantification (evaluation of ten leading models), representation (visualization of self-consciousness within the models), manipulation (modification of the models' representation), and acquisition (fine-tuning the models on core concepts). Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning. Our datasets and code are at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/SelfConsciousness.

papers.title: Discovering and Causally Validating Emotion-Sensitive Neurons in Large Audio-Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether emotion-sensitive neurons exist in large audio-language models, which identification methods are most effective for isolating them, and how these neurons are distributed across layers and transfer across datasets.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides the first neuron-level causal study of emotion-sensitive neurons in large audio-language models, demonstrating their existence and controllability through inference-time interventions.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide causal evidence that compact, emotion-sensitive functional units exist in LALMs and that neuron-level interventions offer a practical handle for interpreting and controlling affective behavior in speech-enabled foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion-sensitive neurons (ESNs) exist in LALMs and can be causally validated via deactivation (ablation) and steering (amplification).
Identification methods based on magnitude (MAD) and contrast (CAS) are more effective at isolating causally emotion-sensitive neurons than frequency (LAP) or entropy (LAPE) based methods.
ESNs are distributed non-uniformly across decoder layers, clustering in early, early-mid, and later layers.
ESNs show partial cross-dataset transferability, with uneven strength across emotions and datasets.
Agnostic injection strategies (2-PASS, MIX, UNION) yield mixed results, hinting at inter-emotion interference among ESNs.
papers.limitation:
The study operationalizes neuron behavior through decoder SwiGLU MLP gate activations and does not characterize how emotion cues are distributed across other components (e.g., attention and audio-text fusion).
Transfer is studied primarily across datasets within speech emotion recognition; generalization across tasks (e.g., expressive speech generation) is not examined.
The paper does not provide a dedicated causal decomposition of inter-emotion interactions among ESNs (e.g., pairwise co-steering).
future_direction: Understanding when emotion-sensitive units generalize across tasks (e.g., expressive speech generation) and how to make steering more uniformly reliable.
Systematic characterization of competitive vs. cooperative affective circuitry among ESNs.
papers.abstract: Emotion is a central dimension of spoken communication, yet, we still lack a mechanistic account of how modern large audio-language models (LALMs) encode it internally. We present the first neuron-level interpretability study of emotion-sensitive neurons (ESNs) in LALMs and provide causal evidence that such units exist in Qwen2.5-Omni, Kimi-Audio, and Audio Flamingo 3. Across these three widely used open-source models, we compare frequency-, entropy-, magnitude-, and contrast-based neuron selectors on multiple emotion recognition benchmarks. Using inference-time interventions, we reveal a consistent emotion-specific signature: ablating neurons selected for a given emotion disproportionately degrades recognition of that emotion while largely preserving other classes, whereas gain-based amplification steers predictions toward the target emotion. These effects arise with modest identification data and scale systematically with intervention strength. We further observe that ESNs exhibit non-uniform layer-wise clustering with partial cross-dataset transfer. Taken together, our results offer a causal, neuron-level account of emotion decisions in LALMs and highlight targeted neuron interventions as an actionable handle for controllable affective behaviors.

papers.title: From Rational Answers to Emotional Resonance: The Role of Controllable Emotion Generation in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to express emotions in a consistent, controllable, and contextually appropriate manner without additional training?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a controllable emotion generation framework using Emotion Vectors (EVs) extracted from internal activation shifts, enabling fine-grained emotional tone modulation in pretrained LLMs during inference without any training.
papers.conclusion: Emotion Vector steering provides an efficient and interpretable means of bridging rational reasoning and affective understanding in LLMs, offering a promising direction for building emotionally resonant AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
EV steering achieves consistent emotional alignment and controllable affect intensity across multiple LLM families.
The method preserves semantic fidelity and linguistic fluency, as measured by topic adherence and perplexity.
Emotional intensity can be linearly controlled by scaling the injected EV, demonstrating predictable behavior.
EV steering outperforms existing prompt-based and fine-tuning-based baselines in flexibility and generalizability.
The method is fully unsupervised, requires no training or architectural changes, and provides global consistency in emotional control.
papers.limitation:
Large norm of extracted EVs in some models (e.g., Llama-3.1) can cause slight degradation in topic adherence.
Very large scaling factors (α) may eventually cause saturation in emotional expression.
papers.abstract: Purpose: Emotion is a fundamental component of human communication, shaping understanding, trust, and engagement across domains such as education, healthcare, and mental health. While large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong reasoning and knowledge generation capabilities, they still struggle to express emotions in a consistent, controllable, and contextually appropriate manner. This limitation restricts their potential for authentic human-AI interaction. Methods: We propose a controllable emotion generation framework based on Emotion Vectors (EVs) - latent representations derived from internal activation shifts between neutral and emotion-conditioned responses. By injecting these vectors into the hidden states of pretrained LLMs during inference, our method enables fine-grained, continuous modulation of emotional tone without any additional training or architectural modification. We further provide theoretical analysis proving that EV steering enhances emotional expressivity while maintaining semantic fidelity and linguistic fluency. Results: Extensive experiments across multiple LLM families show that the proposed approach achieves consistent emotional alignment, stable topic adherence, and controllable affect intensity. Compared with existing prompt-based and fine-tuning-based baselines, our method demonstrates superior flexibility and generalizability. Conclusion: Emotion Vector (EV) steering provides an efficient and interpretable means of bridging rational reasoning and affective understanding in large language models, offering a promising direction for building emotionally resonant AI systems capable of more natural human-machine interaction.

papers.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models possess genuine introspective awareness of their own internal states?
papers.core_contribution: This work demonstrates that large language models have limited, functional introspective awareness, as shown through concept injection experiments where models can detect and report on manipulated internal states.
papers.conclusion: Current language models possess some functional introspective awareness, but it is highly unreliable and context-dependent, and may improve with further model advancements.
papers.key_findings:
Models can sometimes detect injected concepts and accurately identify them, with Claude Opus 4.1 succeeding about 20% of the time in appropriate conditions.
Models can distinguish between injected thoughts and text inputs, performing above chance levels.
Models can use introspection to detect artificially prefilled outputs by recalling prior intentions, as shown in apology experiments.
Models can modulate their internal representations when instructed or incentivized to think about specific concepts.
Introspective capabilities are more pronounced in more capable models like Claude Opus 4 and 4.1, but are unreliable and sensitive to post-training strategies.
papers.limitation:
The abilities observed are highly unreliable; failures of introspection remain the norm.
Experiments do not seek to pin down specific mechanistic explanations for how introspection occurs.
Models often provide additional details about their purported experiences that may be confabulated.
Concept injection protocol places models in an unnatural setting unlike training or deployment.
future_direction: Identifying metacognitive representations more clearly
Exploring how introspection translates to more natural conditions
papers.abstract: Do large language models possess genuine introspective awareness of their own internal states? This work demonstrates that large language models have limited, functional introspective awareness, as shown through concept injection experiments where models can detect and report on manipulated internal states. Current language models possess some functional introspective awareness, but it is highly unreliable and context-dependent, and may improve with further model advancements.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: The Inner Sentiments of a Thought
papers.research_question: How do sentences convey emotional sentiment, and how can we predict and control the emotional trajectory of text using language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for training quantile models to predict the distribution of emotional sentiments from hidden states of a language model, enabling analysis of emotional dynamics in sentences and controlled generation of emotionally targeted text.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that large language models can provide a novel lens onto the inner structure and emotional dynamics of sentences, with a method for predicting sentiment distributions that enables both analysis and controlled generation of emotionally colored text.
papers.key_findings:
Quantile models for predicting emotional sentiment distributions (valence, determination, admiration, anxiety, annoyance) are well-calibrated and accurate.
The predicted quantile trajectories capture intuitive emotional effects, such as the sentiment-reversing role of the conjunction 'but' and the uncertainty-widening effect of intensifiers like 'really'.
The method can be used to steer a language model (GPT-2) to generate text from specific quantiles of an emotional distribution, producing more emotionally colored sentences.
The quantile models rely on the underlying scoring algorithms and dataset, with limitations in capturing the full range of certain emotions from the Reddit data.
The method provides a novel lens for analyzing the inner emotional structure of sentences and has potential applications in areas like psychotherapy and risk-sensitive text generation.
papers.limitation:
Uses a state-of-yesterday's-art language model (GPT-2 large), which is less capable than recent larger models and tends to produce run-on sentences and flaunt grammatical conventions.
The quantile models rely on the underlying scoring algorithms applied to the dataset, which for some emotions were shallow and overly emphasized a small subset of words.
The Reddit dataset appears to be a poor source for capturing the range of certain emotions.
The end sentiment model and emotion classifier predict the probability of text containing a sentiment/emotion, not directly capturing the intensity of emotional expression.
future_direction: Exploring the differences between conditional pretraining/finetuning and online probability-reweighting methods for controlled generation.

Using predictive quantile models to analyze text in a wide variety of ways, complementing lexical analysis and contextualized embeddings, such as searching for phrases with unique emotional dynamics or augmenting lexicon-based analyses of extreme language.
Applying the method to model phenomena like worry and catastrophizing in 'what if' chains-of-thought, and for real-time analysis in psychotherapy to flag cognitive biases.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large-scale language models (LLMs) are able to generate highly realistic text. They are duly able to express, and at least implicitly represent, a wide range of sentiments and color, from the obvious, such as valence and arousal to the subtle, such as determination and admiration. We provide a first exploration of these representations and how they can be used for understanding the inner sentimental workings of single sentences. We train predictors of the quantiles of the distributions of final sentiments of sentences from the hidden representations of an LLM applied to prefixes of increasing lengths. After showing that predictors of distributions of valence, determination, admiration, anxiety and annoyance are well calibrated, we provide examples of using these predictors for analyzing sentences, illustrating, for instance, how even ordinary conjunctions (e.g., "but") can dramatically alter the emotional trajectory of an utterance. We then show how to exploit the distributional predictions to generate sentences with sentiments in the tails of distributions. We discuss the implications of our results for the inner workings of thoughts, for instance for psychiatric dysfunction.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: Preliminary Insights into Affective Modeling in Multimodal Foundation Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal architectural mechanisms that support affective understanding and generation in multimodal foundation models, and do they differ from those used for reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the feed-forward gating projection (gate_proj) as the primary structural locus for affective modeling in multimodal foundation models, showing it is sufficient, efficient, and necessary for affective capabilities, and proposes a gate-focused efficient tuning method (GET) that achieves near state-of-the-art performance with far fewer parameters.
papers.conclusion: Affective capability in foundation models is structurally mediated by feed-forward gating mechanisms, with gate_proj identified as a central architectural locus. This suggests a functional specialization where attention supports structured reasoning while gating regulates affective modulation.
papers.key_findings:
Affective adaptation consistently concentrates on the FFN gating projection (gate_proj) across multiple model architectures, training strategies, and affective tasks.
Selectively transferring only the gate_proj parameters from an affective model to a base model is sufficient to transfer affective capability, yielding stable performance gains.
Fine-tuning only the gate_proj module in isolation is the most efficient and stable adaptation strategy for affective tasks compared to tuning other modules.
Affective performance is governed by functional alignment of adapted modules; indiscriminate tuning of additional modules (e.g., down_proj) can introduce negative transfer and degrade performance.
The proposed Gate-Focused Efficient Tuning (GET) method, which tunes only gate_proj, achieves 96.6% of AffectGPT's average performance across eight affective tasks while tuning only 24.5% of the parameters.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on module-level mechanisms and does not capture finer-grained dynamics at the level of individual neurons, features, or token interactions.
The scope of affective phenomena studied is constrained by available benchmarks, limiting generalization to more diverse emotional states, longer-term affective dynamics, and real-world interactive settings.
The study characterizes how affective capabilities are encoded and functionally expressed after fine-tuning, not how they emerge during large-scale pretraining.
While strong empirical and causal evidence is provided for the role of gate_proj, the work does not present a formal theoretical model explaining why gating mechanisms are particularly well-suited for affective modulation.
future_direction: Investigate how affective signals are distributed within gating dimensions and how they interact with attention patterns at the token level.
Extend the analysis to more diverse emotional states, longer-term affective dynamics, and real-world interactive settings.
Understand whether similar gating-related structures arise spontaneously during pretraining or require explicit affective supervision.
Develop theoretical frameworks explaining why gating mechanisms are well-suited for affective modulation to guide future architecture design and training objectives.
papers.abstract: Understanding where and how emotions are represented in large-scale foundation models remains an open problem, particularly in multimodal affective settings. Despite the strong empirical performance of recent affective models, the internal architectural mechanisms that support affective understanding and generation are still poorly understood. In this work, we present a systematic mechanistic study of affective modeling in multimodal foundation models. Across multiple architectures, training strategies, and affective tasks, we analyze how emotion-oriented supervision reshapes internal model parameters. Our results consistently reveal a clear and robust pattern: affective adaptation does not primarily focus on the attention module, but instead localizes to the feed-forward gating projection (\texttt{gate\_proj}). Through controlled module transfer, targeted single-module adaptation, and destructive ablation, we further demonstrate that \texttt{gate\_proj} is sufficient, efficient, and necessary for affective understanding and generation. Notably, by tuning only approximately 24.5\% of the parameters tuned by AffectGPT, our approach achieves 96.6\% of its average performance across eight affective tasks, highlighting substantial parameter efficiency. Together, these findings provide empirical evidence that affective capabilities in foundation models are structurally mediated by feed-forward gating mechanisms and identify \texttt{gate\_proj} as a central architectural locus of affective modeling.

papers.title: Decoding Emotion in the Deep: A Systematic Study of How LLMs Represent, Retain, and Express Emotion
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to navigate the nuances of human emotion. While research confirms that LLMs can simulate emotional intelligence, their internal emotional mechanisms remain largely unexplored. This paper investigates the latent emotional representations within modern LLMs by asking: how, where, and for how long is emotion encoded in their neural architecture? To address this, we introduce a novel, large-scale Reddit corpus of approximately 400,000 utterances, balanced across seven basic emotions through a multi-stage process of classification, rewriting, and synthetic generation. Using this dataset, we employ lightweight "probes" to read out information from the hidden layers of various Qwen3 and LLaMA models without altering their parameters. Our findings reveal that LLMs develop a surprisingly well-defined internal geometry of emotion, which sharpens with model scale and significantly outperforms zero-shot prompting. We demonstrate that this emotional signal is not a final-layer phenomenon but emerges early and peaks mid-network. Furthermore, the internal states are both malleable (they can be influenced by simple system prompts) and persistent, as the initial emotional tone remains detectable for hundreds of subsequent tokens. We contribute our dataset, an open-source probing toolkit, and a detailed map of the emotional landscape within LLMs, offering crucial insights for developing more transparent and aligned AI systems. The code and dataset are open-sourced.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Emergence Of Emotion Selectivity in A Deep Neural Network Trained to Recognize Visual Objects
papers.research_question: Does emotion selectivity in the visual system arise innately or from reentry from emotion processing structures?
papers.core_contribution: The study demonstrates that emotion-selective neurons spontaneously emerge in a CNN trained for object recognition, and these neurons are functionally significant for emotion recognition, supporting the innate ability of the visual system to represent affective information.
papers.conclusion: Emotion selectivity can spontaneously emerge in a deep neural network trained for object recognition, and these neurons play a functional role in emotion recognition, suggesting that the visual system may have an innate ability to represent affective information.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion-selective neurons exist in all convolutional layers of VGG-16 pretrained on ImageNet.
Emotion selectivity becomes stronger and more consistent in deeper layers of the network.
Lesioning emotion-selective neurons degrades emotion recognition performance, while enhancing them improves performance.
The emotion selectivity is generalizable across different affective image datasets (IAPS and NAPS).
The emergence of emotion selectivity is not due to random chance, as shown by comparison with randomly initialized networks.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the VGG-16 architecture, and results may be model-specific.
It is unclear if emotion selectivity could arise in untrained networks.
Emotion categories are broad (pleasant, neutral, unpleasant), and finer differentiations are not explored.
Caution must be exercised when extending findings from CNN models to the human brain.
future_direction: Examine a broader range of CNN models and other deep neural network architectures.
Investigate whether emotion selectivity can arise in untrained networks.
Explore finer differentiations of emotion categories.
papers.abstract: Visual cortex plays an important role in representing the affective significance of visual input. The origin of these affect-specific visual representations is debated: they are innate to the visual system versus they arise through reentry from frontal emotion processing structures such as the amygdala. We examined this problem by combining a convolutional neural network (CNN) model of the human ventral visual cortex pretrained on ImageNet with two datasets of affective images. Our results show that (1) in all layers of the CNN model, there were artificial neurons that responded consistently and selectively to neutral, pleasant, or unpleasant images and (2) lesioning these neurons by setting their output to 0 or enhancing these neurons by increasing their gain lead to decreased or increased emotion recognition performance respectively. These results support the idea that the visual system may have the innate ability to represent the affective significance of visual input and suggest that CNNs offer a fruitful platform for testing neuroscientific theories

papers.title: Emergence of Emotion Selectivity in Deep Neural Networks Trained to Recognize Visual Objects
papers.research_question: Does emotion selectivity emerge in CNNs trained for object recognition, and are these emotion-selective neurons functionally significant for emotion recognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that emotion-selective neurons spontaneously emerge in CNNs trained for object recognition, and these neurons are functionally significant for emotion recognition, supporting the intrinsic ability of the visual system to represent affective significance.
papers.conclusion: The findings indicate that emotion selectivity can spontaneously emerge in CNN models trained to recognize visual objects, and these emotion-selective neurons play a significant role in recognizing emotion in natural images, lending credence to the notion that the visual system's ability to represent affective information may be intrinsic.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion-selective neurons exist in all layers of CNNs trained for object recognition.
Emotion selectivity becomes stronger in deeper layers.
Emotion-selective neurons generalize across different affective image datasets.
Enhancing emotion-selective neurons improves emotion recognition performance.
Lesioning emotion-selective neurons degrades emotion recognition performance.
papers.limitation:
Emotion was divided into three broad categories; future work should examine finer differentiations.
There might be other factors (e.g., low-level features) that drive emotion selectivity, though color was ruled out and low-level features were analyzed.
The neural relevance is speculative because there is no direct comparison with neural recordings during emotion recognition.
future_direction: Examine finer differentiations of emotion (e.g., joy, sadness, horror, disgust).
Compare activities in deep neural networks with neural recordings during emotion recognition.
papers.abstract: Recent neuroimaging studies have shown that the visual cortex plays an important role in representing the affective significance of visual input. The origin of these affect-specific visual representations is debated: they are intrinsic to the visual system versus they arise through reentry from frontal emotion processing structures such as the amygdala. We examined this problem by combining convolutional neural network (CNN) models of the human ventral visual cortex pre-trained on ImageNet with two datasets of affective images. Our results show that in all layers of the CNN models, there were artificial neurons that responded consistently and selectively to neutral, pleasant, or unpleasant images and lesioning these neurons by setting their output to zero or enhancing these neurons by increasing their gain led to decreased or increased emotion recognition performance respectively. These results support the idea that the visual system may have the intrinsic ability to represent the affective significance of visual input and suggest that CNNs offer a fruitful platform for testing neuroscientific theories.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is it represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs via a single direction in activation space, demonstrates its causal relevance through interventions, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is aggregated at intermediate tokens like commas.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that sentiment is linearly represented and causally relevant in LLMs, identifies a summarization motif, and contributes to understanding internal feature representation, suggesting directions for future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs: a single direction in activation space captures sentiment across tasks and models.
This sentiment direction is causally relevant for sentiment tasks, as shown by activation patching and ablation experiments.
The sentiment direction generalizes across models and out-of-distribution datasets.
The model uses a circuit involving specific attention heads and neurons to process sentiment.
The summarization motif: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens without inherent valence (e.g., commas, periods), acting as information bottlenecks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on decoder-only models, and may not generalize to other architectures.
Toy datasets are simple and may not capture full natural language complexity.
Causal interventions may not fully capture model dynamics on more complex tasks.
future_direction: Extend methods to other features beyond sentiment, such as toxicity or deception.
Investigate the summarization motif in other tasks and models.
Develop more robust methods for finding linear directions in larger models.
papers.abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. Through causal interventions, we isolate this direction and show it is causally relevant in both toy tasks and real world datasets such as Stanford Sentiment Treebank. Through this case study we model a thorough investigation of what a single direction means on a broad data distribution. We further uncover the mechanisms that involve this direction, highlighting the roles of a small subset of attention heads and neurons. Finally, we discover a phenomenon which we term the summarization motif: sentiment is not solely represented on emotionally charged words, but is additionally summarized at intermediate positions without inherent sentiment, such as punctuation and names. We show that in Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, 76% of above-chance classification accuracy is lost when ablating the sentiment direction, nearly half of which (36%) is due to ablating the summarized sentiment direction exclusively at comma positions.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: Structured Self-Attention Weights Encode Semantics in Sentiment Analysis
papers.research_question: Do structured self-attention weights encode semantic information, specifically emotional semantics, in sentiment analysis tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Layer-wise Attention Tracing (LAT), a method to trace attention weights in Transformers, and demonstrates that aggregated attention scores correlate with emotional semantics in sentiment analysis tasks.
papers.conclusion: Structured self-attention weights encode rich semantic information, specifically emotional meaning, in sentiment analysis tasks, and the proposed LAT method provides a way to interpret these weights.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed LAT method can trace attention weights through self-attention layers and aggregate them onto input tokens.
Words with high aggregated attention scores from LAT are rich in emotional semantics, as quantitatively validated by an external emotion lexicon.
A U-shaped quadratic relationship exists between LAT attention scores and emotional valence ratings from the lexicon, indicating high attention for both very positive and very negative words.
Some attention heads specialize in attending to very positive or very negative words, showing emergent specialization.
Attention scores from LAT behave differently from gradient-based importance scores, which do not show a clear quadratic relationship with valence.
papers.limitation:
The attention tracing method is incomplete as it does not take into account the feed-forward layers and residual connections in the encoder.
Attention mechanisms may have identifiability issues, and may not be interpretable in the same way as gradient-based measures.
future_direction: Engineering inductive biases to constrain attention mechanisms for better interpretability.
Further investigation into the debate on whether attention should be interpreted like gradient-based measures.
papers.abstract: Neural attention, especially the self-attention made popular by the Transformer, has become the workhorse of state-of-the-art natural language processing (NLP) models. Very recent work suggests that the self-attention in the Transformer encodes syntactic information; Here, we show that self-attention scores encode semantics by considering sentiment analysis tasks. In contrast to gradient-based feature attribution methods, we propose a simple and effective Layer-wise Attention Tracing (LAT) method to analyze structured attention weights. We apply our method to Transformer models trained on two tasks that have surface dissimilarities, but share common semantics---sentiment analysis of movie reviews and time-series valence prediction in life story narratives. Across both tasks, words with high aggregated attention weights were rich in emotional semantics, as quantitatively validated by an emotion lexicon labeled by human annotators. Our results show that structured attention weights encode rich semantics in sentiment analysis, and match human interpretations of semantics.

papers.title: Curved Inference: A Guide to Geometric Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do token representations evolve geometrically in the residual stream of transformer-based language models, and how does this geometry relate to semantic structure and complex behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Curved Inference framework, a geometric approach to interpretability that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream, demonstrating that these trajectories reflect semantic structure and are associated with behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling.
papers.conclusion: Curved Inference provides a geometric framework for interpretability that shifts focus from static attribution to dynamic inference analysis, offering a model-faithful lens to understand internal computation in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream trajectories are semantically sensitive and show structured curvature in response to concern-shifted prompts.
Residual geometry diverges in cases of latent behavioral shifts, such as deception in sleeper agents, and can precede output changes.
Curvature is functionally associated with sustained self-modeling, persisting even under curvature-penalizing fine-tuning.
Geometric metrics like curvature, salience, and semantic surface area provide reproducible signals across multiple domains.
The residual stream is the exclusive locus for this geometric signal, unlike attention or MLP outputs.
papers.limitation:
Geometric derivatives rely on interpolation assumptions that may not hold in all cases.
Dependence on external LLM classifiers for alignment and intent judgments introduces biases.
Experiments were conducted on models up to 3b parameters, so results may not generalize to larger or opaque systems.
future_direction: Scale testing with larger models
Extending analysis to tasks involving reasoning, planning, or complex dialogue
Formalizing curvature signatures for specific generative behaviors
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a unified framework for analyzing the internal geometry of inference in transformer-based language models. Building on a series of prior studies, we present a consolidated introduction to “Curved Inference”: a methodology that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream as geometric trajectories. Using metrics such as curvature, salience, and semantic surface area, we show that residual trajectories reflect meaningful semantic structure, and are empirically associated with emotional and moral concern, covert intent in sleeper agents, and computational self-modeling dynamics. We consolidate these findings into a reproducible, falsifiable pipeline, supported by formal mathematical definitions and open-source tools. This geometric approach shifts the focus of interpretability from static attribution to dynamic, modelnative inference analysis. The results provide evidence that residual stream geometry is not only measurable, but also structurally related to complex behaviors in the models we study. We invite researchers to replicate, extend, or falsify these claims and test the boundaries of curved inference as a new paradigm for model understanding. Received: 6 August 2025 | Revised: 12 January 2026 | Accepted: 21 January 2026 Conflicts of Interest The author declares that he has no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in GitHub at https://github.com/robman/FRESH-model/tree/main/ benchmarks/curved-inference. Author Contribution Statement Rob Manson: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration.

papers.title: Meanings and Feelings of Large Language Models: Observability of Latent States in Generative AI
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) are observable as dynamical systems, i.e., whether multiple mental state trajectories can yield the same sequence of generated tokens.
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes observability for LLMs and shows that standard autoregressive Transformers are observable, but with hidden system prompts they become unobservable, allowing multiple internal state trajectories to produce the same output.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLMs without system prompts are observable, but with system prompts they are not, and this has implications for security and control of LLM operations.
papers.key_findings:
Standard autoregressive Transformer LLMs without system prompts are observable (the indistinguishable set is a singleton).
With hidden system prompts, LLMs become unobservable, with multiple internal state trajectories yielding the same output.
Empirical validation on GPT-2 and LLaMA-2-7B shows that for Type 1 and Type 2 prompt models, a significant percentage of latent state trajectories are indistinguishable.
Memory models (Type 3 and Type 4) also exhibit unobservability.
Trojan horses can be crafted by optimizing system prompts to produce adversarial outputs after a delay, while remaining indistinguishable initially.
papers.limitation: The analysis does not imply that LLMs are sentient or have feelings in the human sense; it is a formal analogy.
future_direction: Further extensions for the adversarial case and backdoor attacks
Exploring ramifications for security and control of LLM operations
papers.abstract: We tackle the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs), viewed as dynamical systems with state evolving in the embedding space of symbolic tokens, are observable. That is, whether there exist multiple 'mental' state trajectories that yield the same sequence of generated tokens, or sequences that belong to the same Nerode equivalence class ('meaning'). If not observable, mental state trajectories ('experiences') evoked by an input ('perception') or by feedback from the model's own state ('thoughts') could remain self-contained and evolve unbeknown to the user while being potentially accessible to the model provider. Such "self-contained experiences evoked by perception or thought" are akin to what the American Psychological Association (APA) defines as 'feelings'. Beyond the lexical curiosity, we show that current LLMs implemented by autoregressive Transformers cannot have 'feelings' according to this definition: The set of state trajectories indistinguishable from the tokenized output is a singleton. But if there are 'system prompts' not visible to the user, then the set of indistinguishable trajectories becomes non-trivial, and there can be multiple state trajectories that yield the same verbalized output. We prove these claims analytically, and show examples of modifications to standard LLMs that engender such 'feelings.' Our analysis sheds light on possible designs that would enable a model to perform non-trivial computation that is not visible to the user, as well as on controls that the provider of services using the model could take to prevent unintended behavior.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: Attention weights accurately predict language representations in the brain
papers.research_question: Are attention weights in Transformer-based language models related to language representations in the brain? Can attention weights predict brain responses to language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights from Transformer-based language models accurately predict brain responses in language-related cortical areas, and contain information not captured by lexical or contextual embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Attention weights in Transformer-based LMs capture information that is reflected in brain representations during language processing, and indicate cortical areas that could be involved in integrating context across words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 accurately predict brain responses in frontal and temporal cortices associated with language processing.
Attention weights better predict brain responses than lexical embeddings in many language-related areas.
Attention weights from middle layers of BERT explain the most variance in brain responses, consistent with linguistic relevance of middle layers.
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 perform similarly in predicting brain responses, suggesting consistency across unidirectional and bidirectional models.
In some cortical areas, attention weights predict brain responses better than contextual embeddings, indicating additional information in attention weights.
papers.limitation:
The temporal resolution of fMRI (2s) does not capture all the rapid changes in human speech.
Analyses were limited to English language comprehension.
The analyses demonstrate similarity of representations between Transformer-based LMs and brain responses, but do not directly prove the existence of similar underlying computational mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other languages to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of context integration in the brain and in artificial neural networks.

Compare the results of our method of computing attention weights with more cognitively-inspired methods to provide more specific insights into how attention weights in Transformer-based LMs relate to processes in the human brain.
papers.abstract: In Transformer-based language models (LMs) the attention mechanism converts token embeddings into contextual embeddings that incorporate information from neighboring words. The resulting contextual hidden state embeddings have enabled highly accurate models of brain responses, suggesting that the attention mechanism constructs contextual embeddings that carry information reflected in language-related brain representations. However, it is unclear whether the attention weights that are used to integrate information across words are themselves related to language representations in the brain. To address this question we analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings of participants reading English language narratives. We provided the narrative text as input to two LMs (BERT and GPT-2) and extracted their corresponding attention weights. We then used encoding models to determine how well attention weights can predict recorded brain responses. We find that attention weights accurately predict brain responses in much of the frontal and temporal cortices. Our results suggest that the attention mechanism itself carries information that is reflected in brain representations. Moreover, these results indicate cortical areas in which context integration may occur.

papers.title: LLaMAs Have Feelings Too: Unveiling Sentiment and Emotion Representations in LLaMA Models Through Probing
papers.research_question: How are sentiment and emotion representations encoded in LLaMA models, and how can we efficiently extract them for sentiment analysis tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a layer-wise probing method to identify where sentiment and emotion are encoded in LLaMA models, and proposes SENTRI LLAMA, a method that uses only the most representative layers and a lightweight classifier for efficient and accurate sentiment analysis.
papers.conclusion: The layer-wise probing approach reveals where sentiment and emotion are encoded in LLaMA models, and SENTRI LLAMA provides an efficient method for downstream sentiment tasks that outperforms prompting and reduces computational costs.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment concepts are most detectable in mid-layer representations, while emotions are more discoverable in early layers.
The last token is not consistently the most informative for sentiment encoding; alternative pooling methods (e.g., concatenation of mean, max, min) perform better.
Representation quality improves with model size.
Probe classifiers generally outperform prompting techniques for sentiment and emotion classification.
SENTRI LLAMA reduces model size and computational requirements while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.limitation:
The study does not evaluate on domain-specific datasets (e.g., financial, healthcare, social media) or multilingual sentiment analysis, limiting generalizability.
The layer selection mechanism could be improved, e.g., by using only the most representative layer without preceding layers or by incorporating compression/pruning techniques.
future_direction: Systematically evaluate the approach across diverse tasks and datasets to assess generalizability.
Explore extending the method to tasks like sarcasm detection or intent recognition.
Investigate alternative layer selection mechanisms, such as using only the input embeddings and the most representative layer, potentially with compression or pruning.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become central to NLP, demonstrating their ability to adapt to various tasks through prompting techniques, including sentiment analysis. However, we still have a limited understanding of how these models capture sentiment-related information. This study probes the hidden layers of Llama models to pinpoint where sentiment features are most represented and to assess how this affects sentiment analysis. Using probe classifiers, we analyze sentiment encoding across layers and scales, identifying the layers and pooling methods that best capture sentiment signals. Our results show that sentiment information is most concentrated in mid-layers for binary polarity tasks, with detection accuracy increasing up to 14% over prompting techniques. Additionally, we find that in decoder-only models, the last token is not consistently the most informative for sentiment encoding. Finally, this approach enables sentiment tasks to be performed with memory requirements reduced by an average of 57%. These insights contribute to a broader understanding of sentiment in LLMs, suggesting layer-specific probing as an effective approach for sentiment tasks beyond prompting, with potential to enhance model utility and reduce memory requirements.

papers.title: Emergence of psychopathological computations in large language models
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a computational-theoretical framework for psychopathology in AI and provides empirical evidence that LLMs instantiate network-theoretic psychopathological computations.
papers.conclusion: The work provides the first evidence for the emergence of psychopathological computations in LLMs, suggesting that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing, with implications for AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Computational units corresponding to psychopathology symptoms are measurable and causally intervenable within LLM activation space.
These units are connected by a dynamic, cyclic structural causal model (SCM) that exhibits self-sustaining activation patterns.
The computational structure of psychopathology (unit activations and causal links) becomes denser and more effective as LLM size increases.
Activating these units elicits corresponding problematic behaviors in ecologically relevant environments like counseling and gaming simulations.
Joint activation of cycle-forming units creates resistance to prompt-based treatments aimed at suppressing abnormal behaviors.
papers.abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology? An effective approach to the question hinges on addressing two factors. First, for conceptual validity, we require a general and computational account of psychopathology that is applicable to computational entities without biological embodiment or subjective experience. Second, psychopathological computations, derived from the adapted theory, need to be empirically identified within the LLM's internal processing. Thus, we establish a computational-theoretical framework to provide an account of psychopathology applicable to LLMs. Based on the framework, we conduct experiments demonstrating two key claims: first, that the computational structure of psychopathology exists in LLMs; and second, that executing this computational structure results in psychopathological functions. We further observe that as LLM size increases, the computational structure of psychopathology becomes denser and that the functions become more effective. Taken together, the empirical results corroborate our hypothesis that network-theoretic computations of psychopathology have already emerged in LLMs. This suggests that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be a superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing. Our work shows the promise of developing a new powerful in silico model of psychopathology and also alludes to the possibility of safety threat from the AI systems with psychopathological behaviors in the near future.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns.
